options.text: Escalate the incident to the programme board so that it can decide how the two workstreams should co-ordinate and who should own the shared environments.
options.rationale: Co-ordinating workstreams is the programme manager's job, and both leads have asked for exactly that. Escalating a problem you have the authority to solve hands the board a decision it expects you to make.

options.text: Set up a joint planning session each quarter, with a shared dependency board that both workstreams update at every sprint planning and monthly plan review.
options.rationale: Dependencies between workstreams planned on different cycles only surface where the plans meet. A joint session and a shared board create that meeting point, and setting them up is within the programme manager's own remit.

questions.explanation: Workstreams that plan on different cycles, such as a predictive plan and a set of sprints, will miss each other's dependencies unless there is a regular point where their plans are laid side by side. Establishing that integration point, and a shared place to record dependencies between meetings, is part of running an integrated schedule and sits within the manager's own authority. One-way notification rules fix the instance, not the pattern.
questions.mindset: Workstreams planned on different cycles need a place where their plans meet.

questions.stem: You are reviewing the schedule for a multi-storey car park. The precast concrete supplier's factory closes for the first three weeks of August, and the specification prohibits external concrete pours from 1 December to the end of February. The planner has scheduled manufacturing and pours on the standard five-day project calendar, so both restrictions are currently ignored. Which two changes should be made to the schedule model?

options.text: Assign a calendar to the precast manufacturing activities that treats the factory's August shutdown as non-working time.
options.rationale: A resource or activity calendar records when the factory can work, so manufacturing dates move correctly wherever the logic places them, including if the work slips into or out of August.

options.text: Add a 15-day lag after each precast manufacturing activity to allow for the working time lost during August.
options.rationale: A lag adds the delay whether or not the work falls in August. If manufacturing moves a month earlier or later, the lag stays and the schedule becomes wrong in the other direction.

options.text: Assign a calendar to the external pour activities that treats December to February as non-working time.
options.rationale: The winter restriction is about when pours can happen, which is exactly what a calendar models. Any pour the logic pushes into winter then moves to March automatically rather than by hand.

options.text: Set a start-no-earlier-than constraint of 1 March on every external pour activity in the schedule model.
options.rationale: The constraint is right only if every pour would otherwise fall in winter. Pours that could happen in the autumn are pushed to March, and the schedule stops responding to its own logic.

options.text: Add a three-week contingency activity before practical completion to absorb both of the restrictions together.
options.rationale: Contingency is for uncertainty, and these restrictions are known. Lumping them at the end leaves every intermediate date wrong and hides which activities are affected.

questions.explanation: Restrictions on when work can happen belong in calendars, because a calendar lets the network recalculate correctly wherever the logic places an activity. Lags, date constraints and contingency activities each hard-code an assumption about where the work falls, so they are right only until the dates move, which is when the schedule matters most. Known working-time limits are part of the model, not reserve.
questions.mindset: Model when work can happen in calendars, so the schedule still tells the truth after dates move.

questions.stem: Your team builds an insurance broker's quoting portal and also handles production support. Planned velocity is 40 points, but planned work completed has varied between 22 and 38 points over six sprints, because urgent support requests arrive unpredictably and are worked without being recorded. The release forecast still assumes 40 points a sprint. Which two actions will give the team a more reliable forecast?

options.text: Record support requests on the team board as they arrive, so the team can see how much capacity they take each sprint.
options.rationale: Unrecorded work is the reason the forecast keeps missing. Once support is visible the team can measure its typical share of capacity and discuss it with the product owner.

options.text: Estimate each support request in story points and add them to velocity, so that the figure reflects all the work done.
options.rationale: This raises velocity without raising the rate at which the release backlog is burned. The forecast would divide backlog points by a figure that includes work the backlog does not contain.

options.text: Base the release forecast on the planned work actually completed per sprint after support, rather than on the 40-point plan.
options.rationale: The release depends on how fast backlog items are finished, and six sprints show that rate is 22 to 38 points. Forecasting from that range replaces an aspiration with evidence.

options.text: Ask the team to defer non-critical support requests to the following sprint, so the planned 40 points are protected each time.
options.rationale: Deferral may help at the margin, but the requests are described as urgent and the support load does not disappear. The candidate protects the plan rather than correcting the forecast.

options.text: Increase the estimates on all remaining backlog items by a quarter to cover the support work expected in each sprint.
options.rationale: Inflating estimates hides the support load inside the backlog, distorts relative sizing and makes the variation harder to see, not easier to manage.

questions.explanation: A release forecast divides the remaining backlog by the rate at which that backlog is actually being completed. Work that competes for the same capacity but is not recorded makes the planned rate look achievable while the real rate wanders, and the gap appears only as missed dates. Making all demand visible and forecasting from demonstrated throughput on the forecast work are what turn a plan figure into a forecast.
questions.mindset: A forecast is only as honest as the capacity it assumes, so make every claim on that capacity visible.

questions.stem: Your ERP rollout covers 12 countries in predictive deployment waves, with an agile team configuring local variants before each wave. Wave 1 in Portugal took nine weeks instead of the planned seven. The causes were local tax configuration the team had underestimated and a data load that failed once because of a supplier outage. Eleven waves remain, each planned at seven weeks. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Keep the seven-week plan for the remaining waves, since wave 1 was a learning wave and the team should be quicker from now on.
options.rationale: A learning effect is plausible but unproven, and tax configuration differs by country. The candidate keeps the plan on hope while ignoring the only actual data the programme has.

options.text: Re-estimate the remaining waves from wave 1's actual durations, separating the cause likely to recur from the one-off outage.
options.rationale: Actuals from the first unit of repeated work are the best estimating data available. Separating recurring tax complexity from the one-off outage stops the forecast being either too optimistic or too pessimistic.

options.text: Add two weeks to every remaining wave, matching wave 1's overrun so that the plan reflects what the team has just experienced.
options.rationale: Copying the whole overrun forward treats a one-off supplier outage as recurring and assumes every country's tax rules are as complex as Portugal's. It uses the data without analysing it.

options.text: Take the revised forecast through change control if the baseline finish moves, and tell the steering group what the forecast rests on.
options.rationale: If the re-estimate moves the baselined finish, the baseline changes only through governance. Stating the assumptions lets the steering group judge the forecast rather than just receive it.

options.text: Ask the agile team to configure the next three countries in parallel, so the overrun is recovered within the current baseline.
options.rationale: Compressing before re-forecasting commits the team to recovery before anyone knows how large the gap will be, and parallel configuration stretches the team that has just underestimated one country.

questions.explanation: In repeated work, the first unit's actuals are the strongest estimating evidence available, but they have to be analysed before they are applied: causes that will recur belong in every future estimate, while one-off events belong in risk. When the re-estimate moves the baselined end date, the change goes through governance with its assumptions stated, rather than being absorbed silently or promised away.
questions.mindset: Let the first unit of repeated work reset the estimate for the rest, after sorting what will recur from what will not.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme is building a science visitor centre and its ticket-booking app, and different parts of the work reach estimating with very different information behind them. Match each situation to the duration estimating technique that fits it best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: At the feasibility stage, the only information available is how long two similar visitor centres took from groundbreaking to opening.
Electricians will install 3,200 metres of data cabling, and the contractor's records show a crew consistently installs about 160 metres a day.
A first-of-its-kind suspended planetarium dome has never been installed by anyone on the team, and the specialists' views of its duration differ widely.

options.text: Analogous estimating from comparable past projects
options.rationale: With nothing but the totals of similar projects, scaling from those comparisons is the only defensible basis. It is quick and coarse, which suits a feasibility decision.

options.text: Parametric estimating from a reliable unit rate
options.rationale: A known quantity and a consistent productivity rate give a calculable duration: 3,200 metres at 160 metres a day is 20 crew-days. The precision comes from the quality of the rate.

options.text: Three-point estimating from optimistic, most likely and pessimistic views
options.rationale: Novel work with widely differing expert views calls for an estimate that carries its uncertainty. A range built from three points shows the spread instead of hiding it in one figure.

options.text: Relative sizing in story points by the delivery team
options.rationale: Not used. Relative sizing suits backlog items for a stable team with a velocity history to convert points into time. None of the three situations is that, even though the programme includes an app.

questions.explanation: The right estimating technique is set by the information available, not by preference. Comparisons with whole past projects suit early decisions with little detail; a reliable unit rate and a known quantity allow calculation; novel work with disputed durations needs a range that carries the uncertainty. Choosing a precise technique without the data it depends on produces false confidence, and choosing a coarse one when better data exists wastes it.
questions.mindset: Choose the estimating technique the available information can actually support.

questions.stem: Your Scrum team builds a rail operator's journey-planning app and plans at several levels. Match each new piece of information to the planning event where it should be dealt with first. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A rule change means accessibility features must now go in the summer release rather than the autumn one, which reshuffles that release's contents.
On day four of a sprint, a developer finds that a committed story is about twice as large as the team thought, putting the sprint goal at risk.
The marketing lead asks for a new promotional banner feature to be considered for the team's next sprint, which starts in a week.

options.text: Release planning, revisiting the release's scope and order with stakeholders
options.rationale: Moving features between releases changes the release-level plan. It is decided where the product owner and stakeholders weigh release contents, not inside a single sprint.

options.text: The daily scrum, followed by the team re-planning the sprint backlog with the product owner
options.rationale: A threat to the sprint goal discovered mid-sprint is dealt with by the team at its next daily inspection, involving the product owner if scope within the sprint must change.

options.text: Product backlog refinement, where the product owner orders and clarifies new items
options.rationale: A new request first enters the product backlog, where the product owner decides its order and the team makes it ready. Only then can sprint planning consider it.

options.text: The sprint retrospective, where the team inspects how it worked
options.rationale: Not used. The retrospective improves the team's way of working. It may later examine why a story was underestimated, but it is not where any of these pieces of information is first acted on.

questions.explanation: Agile teams plan at nested horizons, from release to sprint to day, and each piece of new information belongs at the horizon whose plan it changes. Changes to release contents go to release planning; threats to the current sprint are handled by the team within the sprint; new requests enter the backlog through the product owner. Taking information to the wrong level either churns plans that did not need to change or delays the ones that did.
questions.mindset: Take new information to the planning horizon it actually changes.

questions.stem: You are setting the progress-measurement rules for a 60 km rural road resurfacing project before status reporting starts. Complete each sentence with the method that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Hundreds of short activities, such as installing a single drainage gully, each take two or three days, well under the weekly reporting period. These should be measured using
Resurfacing is laid lane-kilometre by lane-kilometre, and the site engineer records the quantity laid each day. It should be measured using
Pavement design lasts twelve weeks and passes through defined stages: survey, draft design, independent check and client approval. It should be measured using

options.text: a fixed split, such as 0/100 or 50/50, credited at start and finish
options.rationale: For activities shorter than the reporting period, estimating partial progress adds effort and little accuracy. A fixed split is simple, objective and errs by at most a few days on any one item.

options.text: units completed as a share of the total quantity
options.rationale: Where the work is a measurable quantity recorded daily, progress is simply the share laid. It is objective and leaves no room for optimistic judgement.

options.text: weighted milestones, with a set share credited as each stage is passed
options.rationale: A long activity with defined stages can earn credit at each verifiable stage, which gives regular progress without relying on anyone's sense of how far along the work feels.

options.text: the activity owner's own estimate of percent complete each week
options.rationale: Not used. Subjective estimates tend to run ahead of reality and stall near the end, the familiar pattern of an activity reported 90 percent complete for weeks. Each situation here has a more objective measure.

questions.explanation: Progress measurement should be as objective as the work allows, and the right method depends on the shape of the activity. Short activities are best credited by a fixed rule at start and finish; quantity-based work by units installed; long activities with defined stages by weighted milestones. Subjective percent complete is the method of last resort, because it is where optimistic reporting hides a slip until it can no longer be recovered.
questions.mindset: Measure progress by something you can verify, not by how far along the work feels.

questions.stem: A 1.2 km sewer replacement is planned with overlapping activities. Trenching takes 12 days and starts at the beginning of day 1. Pipe laying takes 10 days and is linked start-to-start to trenching with a 3-day lag. Backfilling takes 6 days and is linked finish-to-finish to pipe laying with a 2-day lag. Days are whole working days numbered from 1.

blanks.label: Day on which pipe laying finishes (at the end of that day)
blanks.rationale: Start-to-start plus 3 means pipe laying can start three days after trenching starts, at the beginning of day 4. Ten days of work from day 4 runs to the end of day 13.

blanks.label: Day on which backfilling starts (at the beginning of that day)
blanks.rationale: Finish-to-finish plus 2 means backfilling finishes two days after pipe laying, at the end of day 15. Counting back six days of work gives a start at the beginning of day 10.

blanks.label: Working days saved compared with running all three activities finish-to-start
blanks.rationale: In strict sequence the work takes 12 + 10 + 6 = 28 days. Overlapped, the last activity finishes at the end of day 15, so the relationships save 28 − 15 = 13 days.

questions.explanation: Start-to-start and finish-to-finish relationships with lags model work that can overlap while keeping a physical spacing between crews. The lag on a start-to-start link counts from the predecessor's start, and on a finish-to-finish link from its finish, so the successor's other date is found by its own duration. The overlap is only as real as the spacing the lag represents; a lag chosen to make the dates fit, rather than to reflect how far ahead one crew must stay, makes the saving fictional.
questions.mindset: Overlap work only as far as the physical spacing between crews really allows.

questions.stem: A publisher's digital team works in Kanban, and its delivery forecasts have slipped for six weeks. Each band of the cumulative flow diagram is labelled with how it has behaved since week 6. Select the stage whose capacity is limiting how fast work reaches Done.

graphic.title: Cumulative flow diagram with five stacked workflow bands over twelve weeks
graphic.caption: Select a band. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between bands, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Backlog: new items arriving steadily at about 8 a week throughout
regions.rationale: Arrivals have not changed, so demand is not what altered in week 6. The backlog explains how much work is waiting to start, not why finished work has slowed.

regions.label: In development: band steady at about 6 items, passing on about 8 a week
regions.rationale: Development is still handing on about eight items a week, matching arrivals. It is keeping pace; if anything it is feeding the queue faster than the next stage can take work from it.

regions.label: Ready for test: band widened from 2 to 18 items since week 6
regions.rationale: This is where the problem is easiest to see, but a queue is the symptom of a constraint downstream, not the constraint itself. Items wait here because the next stage cannot take them.

regions.label: In test: band steady at 3 items, finishing about 4 a week since week 6
regions.rationale: Test is taking in work at the same width but finishing only four a week against eight arriving. That stage's capacity has fallen, which is why the queue in front of it grows and Done has slowed.

regions.label: Done: slope fell from about 8 to 4 items a week since week 6
regions.rationale: The flattening Done line is the outcome being explained. It shows that delivery has halved, but not which stage caused it.

questions.explanation: On a cumulative flow diagram, a band that widens is a queue growing because the stage after it is draining more slowly than work arrives. The constraint is the stage whose exit rate has fallen below the arrival rate, which usually sits immediately downstream of the widening band. Forecasts recover only when that stage's capacity is addressed; starting more work upstream just makes the queue wider.
questions.mindset: Look past where work is piling up to the stage that is not letting it through.
